pedagogy.summary: Extending the formal columnar algorithm from three to four digits. The mathematics is unchanged — align by place value, and compose (carry) or decompose (exchange/borrow) between adjacent columns — but four digits add a thousands column and, crucially, harder exchange chains, including borrowing across one or more zeros (4002-1367). The DfE also requires checking with estimation (rounding) and the inverse, so approximate reasonableness is taught alongside exact procedure.
bestPractices: Keep the base-ten exchange rationale explicit — a carry is 'ten of these make one of those', a borrow is the reverse — do not let it become a symbol-pushing trick
Estimate first by rounding (4002-1367 is about 4000-1400 = 2600) so a place-value slip is caught
Deliberately include one across-zero subtraction — it is the most diagnostic and most-failed case
Use place-value column headers / grid paper so digits of unequal length align correctly (878 under 3456)
Check every answer with the inverse operation
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks including the thousand cube (exchange made physical)
Empty number line for the rounding estimate
commonMisconceptions: Borrow-across-zero failure — cannot decompose when the adjacent column is 0 (4002-1367)
Smaller-from-larger bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position
Misaligns digits when the two numbers have different lengths (right-aligning wrongly, or lining up under the wrong column)
Fails to compose — leaves a two-digit result in a column instead of carrying
Treats checking as redoing the sum rather than estimating or using the inverse

learn.summary: Year 4 pupils extend the formal columnar algorithm from three to four digits: aligning by place value, composing (carrying) when a column total reaches ten or more, and decomposing (borrowing/exchanging) when a top digit is too small — including the hardest case, borrowing across one or more zeros (e.g. 4002-1367). The DfE also requires checking answers by rounding to estimate and by using the inverse operation, so approximate reasonableness is taught alongside the exact procedure. The exchange rationale must stay explicit (a carry is 'ten of these make one of those'; a borrow is the reverse) rather than becoming a symbol-pushing trick.

activities.title: Cascade the thousand: borrow across two zeros with base-ten quantities
feedback: If the child stalls at the zeros or writes a garbled middle (e.g. 3745 or 2735), model exchanging one thousand downward through the columns with base-ten blocks (thousand to ten hundreds to ten tens to ten ones) BEFORE touching the written digits.
If they change the 0 to a 9 but stop borrowing from the next column left, show that the thousand being broken up is what supplies those nines — the 9s and the final 12 all come from one thousand.
If the estimate and exact answer disagree wildly, check for a place-value misalignment rather than redoing blindly.
Confirm success when they treat 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones and reach 2635 with both checks agreeing.
activities.rationale: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in a large diagnostic dataset, and multi-zero minuends compound it across adjacent columns; making the exchange a visible movement of grouped quantities targets exactly where a symbol-only procedure tends to break down. A dynamic or hands-on model lets the child observe the cascade as the thousand-block splits into ten hundreds, then ten tens, then ten ones — the regrouping seen in motion rather than only as a finished state, while a printed worked example can still serve as a static reference.
sourceClaims: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in Brown & Burton's 1325-student data (107 occurrences): when borrowing from a column whose top digit is 0, the student changes the 0 to a 9 but fails to continue borrowing from the next column left; related zero bugs include STOPS/BORROW/AT/ZERO and MOVE/OVER/ZERO/BORROW. Smaller-from-larger (54 students) and these zero-borrow bugs are stable, not careless — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Multi-zero minuends (e.g. 4002) compound the zero-borrow bug across adjacent columns.
Composing/decomposing tens, hundreds and thousands (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods this progression cross-references.
learnerActions: Set up 4002 - 1367 in place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers, aligning from the ones column on the right.
Build 4002 physically (or on a screen model): four thousand-blocks and two ones, with empty hundreds and tens.
Try to subtract 7 ones from 2 ones; notice there is nothing in the hundreds or tens to exchange from, so the exchange must come from the thousands.

Exchange one thousand-block into ten hundred-blocks, then one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones — watching the single thousand ripple down through the two empty columns until the ones column holds 12.
Record each changed digit in the written algorithm in step with the blocks (4002 becomes 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) and finish the subtraction to reach 2635.
Round both numbers to make an estimate (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600). Ideally do this before the exact working in the steps above. Then compare the estimate with the exact answer 2635.
activities.intendedInsight: Borrowing across zero is not a special rule: when an adjacent column is empty you continue the exchange one column further left, and a single thousand can cascade down through the zeros to free up ones. The written digits are a record of quantities actually regrouped.

activities.title: Align and compose: mixed-length columnar addition and subtraction
feedback: If the child lines 878 under the left of 3456, or 483 under the wrong columns of 6250, reinstate place-value headers or grid paper and anchor every number from the ones column on the right.
If they write a two-digit entry such as 14 in the ones column of 3456+878, show that ten ones make one ten carried to the next column.

If they subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (e.g. treat the ones 0-3 as 3 and the tens 5-8 as 3 in 6250-483), stop and exchange concretely: you cannot take 3 ones from 0 ones without exchanging a ten. After that exchange only 4 tens are left, and you cannot take 8 tens from 4 tens without exchanging a hundred.
Confirm success when the ones sit under the ones, carries and exchanges are shown, 3456+878=4334 and 6250-483=5767, and both the estimate and the inverse support each answer.
activities.rationale: Mixed-length alignment and the compose/smaller-from-larger errors are distinct, stable bugs from the borrow-across-zero case, so they deserve their own practice; grid paper and place-value headers give a concrete anchor, and estimation plus inverse checking are statutory.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 4 digits using the formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction where appropriate' and to 'estimate and use inverse operations to check answers to a calculation' (statutory).

Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in Brown & Burton's 1325-student data (107 occurrences): when borrowing from a column whose top digit is 0, the student changes the 0 to a 9 but fails to continue borrowing from the next column left; related zero bugs include STOPS/BORROW/AT/ZERO and MOVE/OVER/ZERO/BORROW. Smaller-from-larger (54 students) and these zero-borrow bugs are stable, not careless — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Multi-zero minuends (e.g. 4002) compound the zero-borrow bug across adjacent columns.
learnerActions: Set out 3456 + 878 using place-value headers or grid paper, placing the 8 of 878 under the ones column (not under the left of 3456).
Add column by column; when the ones make 14, write 4 and carry one ten to the tens column rather than writing a two-digit entry in the ones.
Set out 6250 - 483, anchoring the 3 under the ones column, and subtract, exchanging from the next column left wherever the top digit is too small.
For each answer, round both numbers to estimate first, then check the exact result with the inverse operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Digits are added or subtracted by matching place value, anchored from the ones column on the right regardless of how many digits each number has; a column result of ten or more is carried, and a column that is too small to subtract requires exchanging from the next column left.

activities.title: Check it two ways: estimate and inverse
feedback: If the child simply redoes the original subtraction, scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition separately; do not reteach the algorithm itself.
If the estimate is far from the exact answer, treat that as a signal to re-check alignment or an exchange, not to accept the exact answer anyway.
Confirm success when the child produces a rounded estimate near 2600 AND an inverse sum that returns the original minuend 4002.
activities.rationale: Pupils commonly treat checking as re-running the sum, which cannot catch a systematic procedural bug; the DfE requires both estimation and inverse operations, and separating these from the algorithm keeps them as genuine independent checks.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 4 digits using the formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction where appropriate' and to 'estimate and use inverse operations to check answers to a calculation' (statutory).
learnerActions: After solving 4002 - 1367, round both numbers (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600) on a number line or strip and say whether 2635 is reasonable.
Check the same answer a second, independent way by adding the result to the number subtracted: 2635 + 1367 should return 4002.
Answer: 'What if it had been 4000 - 1367 instead — does that change how you borrow?' and explain.
Compare the two forms of checking and say what each one catches that the other might miss.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking is not redoing the same subtraction: estimation catches place-value-scale slips, and the inverse addition independently confirms the exact answer. They are complementary, not repetition.

constraints: Keep the base-ten exchange rationale explicit throughout — a carry is 'ten of these make one of those', a borrow is the reverse — so the algorithm does not become a symbol-pushing trick.
Deliberately include at least one across-zero subtraction (e.g. 4002-1367): it is the most diagnostic and most-failed case.
Use place-value column headers or grid paper so digits of unequal length align correctly (e.g. 878 under the right-hand end of 3456), anchoring from the ones column on the right.
Estimate first by rounding so a place-value slip is caught, and check every answer with the inverse operation.

A fill-in-the-column or reveal-the-exchange practice format can assess and rehearse the carried/borrowed digits and the rounded estimate, but it cannot verify a child's handwritten column ALIGNMENT, so include some set-it-out-on-paper work where the child chooses the layout.

A tap-to-reveal worked-example reference can show the ten-for-one exchange behind each carry/borrow mark, but it does not let the child perform the exchange, so it supplements rather than replaces active regrouping.

Screen-based base-ten models and physical blocks offer different experiences; either can make the exchange visible, and neither is required over the other. Physical cubes have thickness and can be handled; a screen model is an idealised representation of the same grouped quantities.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified this session. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source attributes '4002-1367 is the single most diagnostic subtraction case' to VanLehn in the assessment field, but the cited full-text source is Brown & Burton (1978); the VanLehn attribution is not backed by a fetched source here and should be checked before asserting it.

One source (NRICH place-value / DfE Appendix 1) is marked verified:false and 'not fetched this session'; it is used to support the exchange rationale in activity 1, so treat that support as unverified.

Original source fields contained comparative-necessity phrasing ('which no static picture can', 'a genuine third dimension adds nothing', open dialogue 'cannot exercise' the task). These have been softened to scoped affordances/limits; no comparative efficacy of one medium over another is established by the available sources.
The original pedagogy listed a part-whole bar model representation that is not used in these activities; it was a non-central representation, not an error.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4002-1367=2635 (regrouping 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) is correct; 2635+1367=4002 confirms. 3456+878=4334 (ones 6+8=14, write 4 carry 1). 6250-483=5767. Rounded estimate 4000-1400=2600 is close to 2635. All checked consistent.

probeDeeper: Roughly what should the answer be, before you work it out exactly?
Why did you have to change the top number in the tens and hundreds when subtracting 4002 - 1367?
What if it had been 4000 - 1367 instead - does that change how you borrow?
How could you use addition to check your subtraction is right?
assess.correctAnswer: Aligns each sum by place value (878 under the right-hand end of 3456; 483 under the ones/tens/hundreds of 6250), composes tens/hundreds/thousands when carrying, and exchanges correctly across BOTH zeros in 4002-1367 (treating 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) to get 2635. Estimate approx 4000-1400 = 2600, close to 2635; inverse 2635+1367 = 4002.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot decompose to subtract in 4002-1367 because the hundreds and tens are 0 (borrow-across-zero) - writes a garbled answer or stalls at the zeros
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model exchanging one thousand downward through the columns with base-ten blocks (thousand to ten hundreds to ten tens to ten ones) BEFORE touching the digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer wrong in the middle columns (e.g. 3745, 2735), or the child freezes / puts 0s where a borrow was needed

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of which is on top (smaller-from-larger bug), e.g. in 6250-483 does 3-0 or 0-3 as 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Concrete exchange on the failing column; 'you cannot take 8 from 5 tens without exchanging a hundred'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column results are 'flipped' wherever the top digit is smaller than the bottom

errorPatterns.pattern: Misaligns digits when the numbers are different lengths - lines 878 under the left of 3456, or 483 under the wrong columns of 6250
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use place-value headers or grid paper; anchor from the ones column on the right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column setup on paper - the ones do not sit under the ones

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves a two-digit result in a column instead of carrying (fails to compose), e.g. writes 12 in the ones of 3456+878
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show ten ones = one ten carried to the next column; base-ten regroup.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An un-carried two-digit entry in the written work

errorPatterns.pattern: When asked to check, simply redoes the same sum rather than estimating or using the inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition; do not reteach the algorithm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The check step reproduces the original method instead of an independent estimate/inverse

responseLevels.gap: Misaligns the digits or breaks down at the zeros; has no sense of whether the answer is reasonable.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three including the double-zero borrow, aligns correctly, AND verifies with both an estimate and the inverse; transfers the method to 4000-1367.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the clean items right and can describe the column steps, but fails the across-zero exchange, or checks only by redoing the sum and never estimates.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three to set out and solve on paper, watching how they line the digits up: 3456 + 878; 4002 - 1367; 6250 - 483. Then ask them to check the 4002 - 1367 answer two ways - by estimating and by the inverse.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 4002-1367 forces a double borrow across two zeros - the single most diagnostic subtraction case (VanLehn). 3456+878 forces multi-column composing, and 6250-483 forces alignment of a three-digit number under a four-digit one. A shallow procedure fails visibly at the zeros or the alignment while sailing through the clean addition.
